Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

comdynamite (development version)

  • abc_choose() chooses among models with a classification random forest (Pudlo et al. 2016) and reports the out-of-bag error and confusion matrix; predict() gives the chosen model, the votes and its posterior probability. abc_ppc() runs posterior predictive checks after abc_fit(), from the reference table or with new simulations, and gives a two-sided posterior predictive p-value per statistic. data-raw/abc_model_choice.R tests both on phylogenetic competition against no competition: the models were told apart with an out-of-bag error of 0.04, while the check on temporal statistics had little power, since the competition model contains the neutral one.
  • Inference by approximate Bayesian computation with random forests (Raynal et al. 2019), with abcrf in Suggests. abc_table() draws parameters from uniform priors and simulates a reference table, abc_fit() fits one regression forest per parameter, predict() gives the posterior median and a credible interval for observed statistics, abc_importance() ranks the statistics, and abc_recovery() measures R2, bias and coverage in pseudo-observations left out of the table. data-raw/abc_recovery.R repeats the design of the ABC pilot: the forests recovered the parameters about as well as rejection ABC at its best tolerance, without having to choose one, with calibrated or conservative intervals.
  • plot() of pcps_test() has a clades argument. It takes either the number of the deepest clades of the tree or a vector of clade names, such as families, named by species, and draws the species as stars coloured by clade, each clade with its convex hull and name, as in Fig. 1 of Debastiani & Duarte (2014). With clades, the predictor fills the sites. Sites are now drawn below the species. pcps_test() keeps the pruned tree as tree.
  • The article “Testing the whole tree” cites the origin of the principal coordinates of phylogenetic structure and explains why the curve of phylogenetic signal of the package PCPS (pcps.curve()) is not implemented.
  • The article “Rates and assembly” rejects ES-sim at p ≤ 0.05, the rule of the preprint, instead of p < 0.05. With 999 null draws five cells change by one replicate each and no conclusion changes.

comdynamite 0.7.0

  • New article “Does metacommunity assembly leave a trace in branch rates?”, a recovery study with planted signals. Branch rates are weakly identified. Partner turnover planted in the rates is barely recovered among species, but local adaptation and character displacement are recovered among populations. The T-statistics compensate when both act, and displacement is identifiable only when the competition kernel is not much narrower than the spacing of species. With fully sampled clades, a PGLS of DR on metapopulation persistence, as in Januario et al. (2025), has no power under a causal link, whereas ES-sim on turnover has. Simulations are in data-raw/bridge_*.R and data-raw/januario_*.R.

  • simulate_metacommunity() and mc_dynamics() record the colonisation history of every population present at the last step: arrival (the step of the last founding, reset by recolonisation after local extinction; 1 for populations present from the start), propagule (the number of founders), immigrants (immigrants and seeds since arrival) and migrant_load (the summed share of newcomers in the population since arrival), all sites x species matrices, plus n_steps. No random draws are added, so abundances are unchanged for the same seed. colonisation_history() returns them as a table.

  • sample_individuals() has two arrival-dependent population deviations, both off by default (which keeps earlier results for the same seed):

    • founder_sd: founder effects, a deviation drawn at colonisation with standard deviation founder_sd / sqrt(founders) that persists and is eroded by gene flow by exp(-gene_flow * migrant_load);
    • monopolization: evolution-mediated priority effects (Urban & De Meester 2009), in which a population closes the gap between the optimum of its species and the environment of its site at a rate per step since its arrival, toward a balance between selection and migration set by gene_flow. Early colonists end up better matched to their site than late arrivals. With either, the result gains an arrival column. Neither feeds back on the dynamics.

  • nested_variance() has a crossed argument for a second hierarchy crossed with factors, such as genus > species crossed with region > site, with a level for the interaction of the finest levels (the population, species by site; interaction = TRUE). When species occur at several sites, a nested factors = c("region", "site", "species") makes species the population and mixes differences among species with differences among populations; in a simulation with 82% of the variance among species and 9% among populations, the nested model gave 88% to species, the crossed one 78% and 11%. The crossed-factors warning now points to crossed. Crossed models, and nested ones that nlme::lme() fails to fit, are fitted with lme4::lmer() (new in Suggests); singular fits warn, and the attributes singular and engine record them.

  • trait_gradient_test() has two nulls for conserved niches: null = "phylo", the phylogenetic permutations of Lapointe & Garland (2001), in which species means move preferably among relatives, and null = "bm", means simulated by Brownian motion. In simulations where the trait and the niches both evolve along the tree, the phylogenetic permutations bring the error from 14–23% (exchange among all species) to 2–11%; "bm" is exact there but fails for traits without phylogenetic structure.

  • trait_gradient_bayes() fits in Stan (through cmdstanr, in Suggests) a bivariate phylogenetic mixed model in which the position of species along the gradient (beta) and their mean trait are latent effects estimated from every site. It returns the phylogenetic share lambda of beta, alpha and the mean with credible intervals, the phylogenetic correlations, species values and convergence diagnostics. Lambda has its own prior (lambda_prior, uniform by default) instead of the U-shaped prior implied by independent priors on two standard deviations; ou_alpha gives an OU structure with a given strength; pp_check() works on the result. In simulations with about 40 species it recovered lambda near 0 and 1, and estimated intermediate lambda low with wide intervals (see Limits).

  • trait_gradient() runs the trait-gradient analysis of Ackerly & Cornwell (2007): each species’ trait splits into its position along the gradient of community trait means (beta) and its difference from co-occurring species (alpha), with niche breadth and the slope within species. Changes from the original:

    • Site means leave out the focal species by default, which removes the circularity that inflates the correlation of beta with the species mean and with alpha; leave_one_out = FALSE reproduces the original script.
    • The weights of site means and of species means are chosen separately; trait_gradient_weights() compares the four combinations.
    • trait_gradient_test() exchanges the trait means of species among species by default, keeping the communities as observed; a curveball null (richness of sites and frequency of species fixed) and the original permutation are options. In simulations, the variance tests under the curveball and the original permutation reject far too often when species turn over along the gradient, so they are for the correlation of beta and alpha only.
    • trait_gradient_phylo() fits a model without phylogeny, Brownian motion and an OU process to beta, alpha and the species mean by REML, with the bootstrap standard errors of each value added to the covariance, and compares them by AIC.
    • plot() draws the gradient, beta against alpha, or the null distributions.

  • population_shifts():

    • The grid of kernel widths no longer goes below the pooled standard deviation within populations, and a warning is given when the best width is at an end of the grid or the fit barely changes along it.
    • env takes several environmental variables, and species_slopes = TRUE gives each species its own slope.
    • community (a site x species matrix of abundances) lets species that were present but not measured push the populations measured at their sites, with the mean of their populations elsewhere moved along the gradient by the fitted slopes.
    • nboot runs a parametric bootstrap of the design. It gives a p-value for displacement that accounts for the choice of the width and is centred on the mean of the simulations without displacement, a first-order bias correction of c, and intervals for c and the slopes. The simulations without displacement come from the fit without displacement, the species constants from the populations that enter the fit, and the variance of populations from a moment equation weighted by precision. Taking the slopes of the full fit inflated that variance and the bias of c under the null, so the test rejected too often in large designs (up to 29% at the 5% level in the experiments of data-raw/bridge_experiments.R). The test is now somewhat conservative (about 2–3% at the 5% level in simulations without displacement), because the centre of the null simulations follows the estimate.
    • The documentation now gives the sign of the bias that deviations of whole populations cause in c: upward when most competitors are closer than w in trait, downward when most are farther.
    • plot() draws the profile of R², c and h along the width.

  • All plots now use ggplot2 (in Suggests, version 3.5.0 or later) and return a ggplot object, which can be changed further with ggplot2: plot_node_test() (both layouts), plot_node_heatmap(), plot_trait_partition(), plot_phylo_beta(), plot_traits(), plot() of rate_matrix(), plot_assembly(), plot() of food_web_dynamics() and the frames of animate_food_web(). Tables these functions used to return invisibly are kept as attributes (marks, values, fractions, ordered). Colours are colours and text sizes text_size everywhere; col, cex, lwd and logical labels (now tip_labels or species_labels) still work, with a warning, until 1.0.0. legend is TRUE or FALSE; a position keyword is still accepted. Arguments of base graphics passed in ... are no longer used.

  • Renamed for consistency; the old names still work, with a warning, until 1.0.0: traits_ou() is now trait_ou() (like trait_bm(), trait_mk() and trait_rates()); fit_damocles() is now damocles_fit(); the nperm argument of tstats() and community_index() is now n_perm, as in the rest of the package; trait_rates(root_value) is now root, as in trait_ou(); trait_mk(root) is now root_state, since it is a state; plot() of trait_rarefaction() takes colours, as the other plots. trait_rates() returns the rates as edge_rates, as trait_mk() does (edge_rate is kept until 1.0.0).

  • tstats_summary(level = ) is now the coverage of the null distribution (default 0.95), as in null_intervals() and plot() of tstats(); values below 0.5 are read as the size of the test, as before, with a warning.

  • plot_rates() draws any rate per branch on the tree, from trait_rates(), history_rates(), turnover_rates(), food_web_rates() or an estimator, with ggplot2. plot() for pcps_test() draws the sites on two principal coordinates, coloured by a predictor, with the species as arrows; pcps_test() now also returns share, species and env for it. The vignette “Rates of trait evolution that vary among branches” and the article on the whole tree use them.

  • Clearer errors: functions that take a tree say so when given something else, instead of repeating a failed condition, and species_traits(), competition_matrix(), assemble_community(), sample_individuals(), tstats(), community_index() and trait_rarefaction() name the argument at fault. damocles_loglik() and the functions that call it stop when no species of comm is a tip of the tree.

  • Help pages link to the other functions of their group (@family), following the groups of the reference index. The example of paint_regimes() uses a tree from treeshapesim.

  • Plots for several traits, in base graphics: plot_traits() draws traits from traits_ou() with their tree, as a phylomorphospace (two traits) or a traitgram (one trait), with branches coloured by regime and the colour changing where a mapped history changes; plot() for rate_matrix() draws each regime’s rate matrix as an ellipse; plot_assembly() draws a community from assemble_community() in trait space, with the boundary of the filter or the contours of limiting similarity in the metric of the assembly. New article, “Correlated traits and assembly in trait space”.

  • traits_ou(): theta can be a matrix with one column per trait, so that a regime shifts each trait’s optimum by its own amount; root can have one value per trait and is checked; a mapped history is matched to the tree by its edges, so it may come in another order of edges. A named theta or sigma2 of length one is no longer recycled to every regime: it must name every regime, as before rate matrices were added.

  • rate_matrix() returns an object of class rate_matrix, with print() and plot() methods. assemble_community() returns an object of class mc_assembly, which keeps the rule, distance, optimum, traits and the matrix of the metric, with a print() method; it stops on missing or non-numeric traits instead of keeping such species or failing later.

  • The limiting-similarity rule of assemble_community() keeps the nearest neighbour of each species up to date instead of scanning the whole distance matrix at each removal: 23 times faster for a pool of 2000 species reduced to 100 (from 10.6 to 0.46 s), with the same species removed and the same random draws.

  • Simulations with a niche of several axes keep their tree. as_mc_data() keeps one column of optima per axis, summary_stats() uses the first axis, and sample_individuals() stops with a clear message; both use the env that set growth when simulate_metacommunity(env = ) was given one. Axes of env without names take the names of the list of traits, or axis1, axis2, …

  • Plots of null-model tests: plot() for tstats() and community_index() draws, site by site, the null interval (hatched by default) with the observed value coloured by the test, or the standardised effect sizes; null_intervals() returns the table behind it.

  • trait_densities() gives trait probability densities of populations and communities (Carmona et al. 2016, 2019) with one bandwidth for all populations, and plot_population_traits() draws them with adjustable transparency. trait_densities() warns when the spread within populations rises with their mean (one bandwidth then fits badly; the logarithm of the trait usually helps), and plot_population_traits(highlight = ) draws a few species in colour and the rest in grey, for sites with many species.

  • Classic metrics of trait spacing and spread, for use with community_index(): mnnd(), sdnnd(), cvnnd(), min_nnd(), max_nnd(), mnd(), sdnd(), cvnd(), mst_length(), mst_ratio(), trait_range(), trait_kurtosis() and nn_distances(). Zero distances count (cati discards them), and one-trait metrics use sorted values instead of distance matrices.

  • community_index() accepts a named list of indices, computed on the same randomised communities, and returns them in one table with an index column.

  • Sampling effort: sample_individuals() gains cover (measure only the most abundant species of each site, as in Pakeman & Quested 2007) and min_n; subsample_individuals() applies the same schemes to real data, and trait_rarefaction() follows any statistic over the number of individuals per population or over cover, with a plot() method that marks the 80% rule of Pakeman & Quested (2007) with a dashed line. Its default statistic computes the T-statistics without permutations.

  • tstats(): the null model of T_IC.IR now keeps the observed regional variance as the denominator. It was computed from the values drawn, which repeat individuals across sites; this biased the null upward and made the tests anti-conservative (about 6% of sites rejected per tail at a nominal 4% in simulations with random traits).

  • New functions for analyses of intraspecific trait variation, written from the published definitions to replace functions of cati 0.99.6 that give wrong results (an audit found bugs reported as adrientaudiere/cati#13 to #21): tstats_summary() summarises the tests of tstats() (shares of sites below and above the null, test of the mean over sites, the sites that deviate), with sites that cannot be tested left out instead of given small p-values; trait_flex() splits community-weighted means into species turnover, intraspecific variability and covariation (Lepš et al. 2011), with environmental variables matched to sites by name, and a plot() method (ggplot2) with explained and residual sums of squares; nested_variance() gives REML variance components across nested levels (nlme in Suggests) and stops when the factors are not ordered from the broadest to the finest level, with a plot() method that draws stacked bars of the shares in Okabe-Ito colours (ggplot2 in Suggests); community_index() compares any trait index of communities with four null models, with all traits of an individual kept together in multivariate indices. The standardised effect size is now NA when the null values do not vary, as for an index that a randomisation cannot change.

  • population_shifts() estimates local adaptation (h) and character displacement (c) together from the population means of individuals, by a regression within species on the environment of the site and on the push predicted from co-occurring competitors, with the individuals of each population split in halves against the bias of sampling error and the kernel width profiled. tstats(null_ip = "species") adds a null model for T_IP.IC that exchanges population means among the populations of each species, so that its effect size is near zero when the site does not matter, positive under convergence and negative under divergence; the null model of Taudiere & Violle (2016) is far below zero for any set of distinct species. In data-raw/pilot_tstats_identifiability.R (ABC, h ~ U(0, 1), c ~ U(0, 10), ten individuals per population, metacommunities of the pseudo-observations left out), the T-statistics alone recover h (R2 0.87 to 0.89 over tolerances) but hardly c (0.56 to 0.58), while the estimates of population_shifts() recover both (0.99, and 0.95 to 0.96; recoverable at tolerance 0.05). group_sum(), used inside tstats(), now gives zero to empty groups, and tstats() no longer fails on a trait without values.

  • sample_individuals(displacement = , displacement_width = ) adds character displacement: the populations of each site sit at the equilibrium between selection toward their mean without competitors and a push away from close competitors through a Gaussian competition kernel, weighted by their abundance. tstats() now has the three null models of Taudiere & Violle (2016) in base R (nperm, alternative), with standardised effect sizes and p-values, so cati is needed only for comparison. The null model for T_IP.IC in cati::Tstats() 0.99.6 puts together permutations of different sites, so its effect sizes for T_IP.IC are wrong (adrientaudiere/cati#12); its regular-expression match of site names was also reported upstream (adrientaudiere/cati#11). In data-raw/demo_tstats.R, character displacement lowers T_IP.IC and raises T_PC.PR and offsets local adaptation: with local_adaptation = 0.9, displacement = 10 takes T_IP.IC from 0.61 to 0.011 and T_PC.PR from 0.010 to 0.59.

  • New vignette “Rates of trait evolution that vary among branches” (branch-rates): rates as a model (trait_rates()), from a history along the tree (history_rates()) and from ecological dynamics (turnover_rates(), food_web_rates()), and how well two estimators recover them, computed in advance by data-raw/vignette_rates.R. RRphylo follows the change that happened on each branch (mean Spearman rho 0.35 to 0.37) but hardly the true rate (0.06 to 0.08, against a ceiling of 0.24 to 0.35 set by one realisation per branch); Brownian motion with regimes in mvMORPH recovers the ratio between the rates of two habitats (medians 1.02, 2.12 and 5.46 for true ratios 1, 2 and 5); and the RRphylo rates of tip branches follow the turnover of partners weakly (median rho 0.10).

  • fit_damocles(shared = TRUE) and damocles_test(shared = TRUE) estimate one pair of DAMOCLES rates for several communities on the same tree from the sum of their log-likelihoods. A single community rarely holds enough information on colonisation and extinction; pooling communities narrows the estimates (data-raw/validation_damocles.R), provided they can be treated as independent realisations of the process.

  • damocles_samples() fits DAMOCLES rates over a list of configurations of regimes or edge covariates, such as posterior samples of rate shifts or of branch-specific rates of speciation, and summarises how often they beat constant rates, the parameters that mean the same in every fit, and the rate of each edge. damocles_partition_test() tests a partition against random partitions of the same complexity placed elsewhere on the tree, drawn by random_regimes() (max_overlap excludes placements that nearly coincide with the one tested), which asks whether the partition is better placed than arbitrary ones rather than only whether rates vary; with the effect in another clade, the chi-squared test rejected constant rates in 29 of 40 replicates and this test in none. clade_regimes() also takes node numbers. dr_rates() computes the tip diversification rate DR of Jetz et al. (2012), per tip or per edge, to use as an edge covariate. data-raw/damocles_bamm.R and data-raw/damocles_clads.R show the path from BAMM (BAMMtools) and ClaDS (RPANDA) output to these functions; with continuous rates, single posterior samples attenuate the slope, so the help recommends fitting the posterior summary of each rate.

  • DAMOCLES rates can change across the tree. simulate_damocles() and damocles_loglik() take one rate per edge; fit_damocles() and damocles_test() estimate rates that differ among regimes of the edges or change with an edge_covariate, for colonisation, extinction or both (vary). Regimes can be clades defined a priori (clade_regimes()) or rate shifts from methods of diversification (BAMM, ClaDS and similar), given as plain vectors so that no such package is needed. damocles_lrt() compares nested fits (constant against varying rates, shared against separate, allopatric against estimated sympatry) and confint() gives profile-likelihood intervals. Type I error and power of the comparison with constant rates are in data-raw/validation_damocles.R.

  • simulate_damocles(), damocles_loglik(), fit_damocles() and damocles_test() take sympatry, the probability that a locally present ancestor leaves both daughters present at speciation (in situ speciation, or recolonisation before the daughters diverge), relaxing the strictly allopatric rule of Pigot & Etienne (2015), which stays the default (sympatry = 0). The likelihood remains exact; fit_damocles(sympatry = NULL) estimates it, which needs several communities with shared rates (data-raw/validation_damocles.R).

  • food_web_rates() turns the rates of trait change of the resource, consumer and predator from food_web_dynamics() into rates per branch for trait_rates(edge_rates = ): each tip belongs to a trophic level, and over the last window units of time of its branch the rate is sigma2 * (1 + k * speed), where speed is the mean rate of change of the mean trait of that level while present. As in turnover_rates(), only tip branches are informed; the speeds are directional changes under selection, so they give relative rates among levels, not Brownian variances.

  • Community assembly with several traits. assemble_community(distance = ) measures trait space by Euclidean distance ("euclidean", the default and the earlier behaviour), Euclidean distance on traits standardised by their standard deviation in the pool ("standardized"), or Mahalanobis distance with the covariance of the pool or a given trait_cov ("mahalanobis"), in both limiting similarity and filtering; filtering by Mahalanobis distance is filtering by a multivariate Gaussian niche. The help explains when each fits: Euclidean distances count correlated traits more than once. growth_rates() and simulate_metacommunity() take a niche with several environmental axes: a list of traits, one per axis, and, in simulate_metacommunity(env = ), a matrix with one column per axis; the growth rate is the product of the responses to each axis, as in simulate_static().

  • traits_ou() simulates several correlated traits: sigma2 can be an evolutionary rate matrix, or a named list with one matrix (or one rate) per selective regime, as in the multi-rate models of mvMORPH (Clavel et al. 2015). regimes can also be a mapped history (class simmap, such as from trait_mk()), so that regimes, optima and rates change within branches. With one number as sigma2 the values are the same as before for the same seed. rate_matrix() builds rate matrices with the structures that mvMORPH::mvBM() fits: any matrix ("default"), independent traits ("diagonal", "equaldiagonal"), equal rates with correlations ("equal"), and, across regimes, proportional matrices ("proportional"), shared eigenvectors ("shared"), equal variances ("variance") or equal correlations ("correlation"). data-raw/validation_mvtraits.R checks them against mvMORPH 1.2.3: over 20000 simulations with two regimes changing within branches, the covariances of the tips stayed within 2.9 Monte Carlo standard errors of sum_k kronecker(R_k, C_k) (mvSIM: 2.8), and under OU within 3.1 of the covariance of Hansen (1997); mvBM() with the same constraint recovered the matrices (100 tips, median of 30 fits within 9% of each true element).

  • sample_individuals() draws individuals from the populations of a simulated metacommunity, with trait values made of the optimum of the species, a fraction of the gap to the environment of the site (local_adaptation), a deviation of the population that does not track the environment (population_sd) and variation among individuals (intraspecific_sd). tstats() computes the T-statistics of Violle et al. (2012) per site, in base R for the observed values or through cati::Tstats() (Taudiere & Violle 2016, now in Suggests) for its null models; both give the same values. Sites are passed to cati under labels of equal width, because cati::Tstats() matches site names as regular expressions and would pool site1 with site10. data-raw/demo_tstats.R shows that local adaptation raises T_IP.IC (from 0.02 to 1.0 as it goes from none to complete) and lowers T_IC.IR and T_PC.PR (from 0.54 and 0.89 to below 0.01), means of 20 metacommunities.

  • simulate_damocles(), damocles_loglik(), fit_damocles() and damocles_test() implement the dynamic null model of community assembly of Pigot & Etienne (2015, DAMOCLES): each lineage colonises the local community at rate gamma and goes locally extinct at rate mu along the tree, and at each allopatric speciation a present ancestor leaves one present daughter. The likelihood follows the pruning algorithm of the article, the rates are fitted by maximum likelihood with optim(), and damocles_test() compares MPD and MNTD of each community with communities simulated under the fitted rates and with random draws of the same richness. All is base R, from the published equations. data-raw/validation_damocles.R checks it against the DAMOCLES package (2.3): log-likelihoods matched DAMOCLES_loglik() to 3e-14 in 180 comparisons (20 trees, three pairs of rates, three priors at the root, some trees with a root edge); maximum likelihoods matched DAMOCLES_ML() to 5e-4 in ten communities, ours equal or higher in all; and over 4000 simulated communities per setting the frequency of presence of each of 40 tips, the mean richness, MPD and MNTD agreed with DAMOCLES_sim() (largest difference in a tip frequency 0.032, |z| < 3). The rates themselves are poorly identified from one community of 60 species (true gamma = mu = 1; estimated mu from zero to thousands).

  • partner_turnover() counts, for each species of a simulated metacommunity, the entries and exits of other species (all of them, or only competitors) in the sites it occupies, per site and time step between recorded steps. turnover_rates() turns this turnover into rates per branch for trait_rates(edge_rates = ), sigma2 * (1 + k * turnover) over the last window units of time of each tip branch, linking the assembly of the metacommunity to rates of trait evolution (evolution speeds up as the community around a lineage changes). The simulation runs among the tips in ecological time, so only tip branches are informed and the match between ecological and branch time is set by window.

  • plot.food_web() draws the abundances, mean traits and rates of trait change from food_web_dynamics() in stacked panels, with introductions marked; with time it draws the state up to that time on the axes of the whole run. animate_food_web() turns these frames into a GIF (gifski in Suggests); the reference page of food_web_dynamics() shows one, made by data-raw/food_web_gif.R.

  • food_web_dynamics() simulates the joint dynamics of abundances and mean traits of a resource, a consumer and a predator, the three-trophic-level model of chapter 3 of McPeek (2017, Evolutionary Community Ecology): quadratic intrinsic rates, Holling type II feeding, optional omnivory, and attack coefficients that are Gaussian, logistic or Michaelis-Menten functions of the traits. Mean traits follow the selection gradients, computed numerically from the fitness of a phenotype among individuals at the mean; everything is integrated by a fixed-step Runge-Kutta method in base R. Levels can be absent or introduced at given times, and the output keeps the selection gradients and the rates of trait change, for later use as rates per lineage. food_web_params() holds the parameters with the names of the book. data-raw/validation_food_web.R reproduces figure 3.2 (consumer peak of 10.2 at iteration 198, final traits 17.1 and 15.6, attack coefficient 0.091, rates of trait change 280 and 47 times lower at iteration 3000 than at their maxima), figure 3.3 (the consumer at a maximum and the resource at a minimum of their fitness surfaces at the end) and the effect of the predator in figure 3.11: with the predator the resource evolves a trait closer to its birth optimum of 12 under the three attack forms, from 16.8 to 11.8 with Gaussian attack (book: 15.6 to 12.4), from 13.6 to 12.6 with logistic attack (15.4 to 12.9) and from 10.1 to 11.6 with Michaelis-Menten attack (10.1 to 11.5). The three-level Michaelis-Menten panel is reproduced closely; the consumer and predator traits of the logistic panel cannot be reproduced from the parameters of its caption, at which the consumer cannot persist. Against the MATLAB code of the resource-consumer models published with McPeek (2017, The American Naturalist), the fitness functions and gradients are the same and the trajectories of figure 3.2 agree within 1e-4 of the author’s ode45 integration; that code has no predator, and the chapter’s own code was offline and not archived. trait_floor keeps mean traits at or above a value, as the author’s code does at zero (the default with Michaelis-Menten attack).

  • history_rates() turns the history of a discrete character along the tree, such as the region or habitat of each lineage from trait_mk() or a stochastic map, into the rate of each branch for trait_rates(edge_rates = ): a rate per state ("state"), a burst after each change that decays exponentially ("burst"), or a rate that depends on the number of lineages in the same state ("sympatry", as in the diversity-dependent model with biogeography of Drury et al. 2016). The rate of a branch is its mean over time. data-raw/validation_sympatry.R checks "sympatry" against RPANDA: the covariance matrices of the tips matched those of the diversity-dependent model with biogeography to 3e-15 in 30 stochastic maps, and RPANDA::fit_t_comp() recovered r from traits simulated with these rates (60 tips, three regions; mean estimate -0.30 for a true -0.3, 80% of estimates between -0.32 and -0.27, and 0.005 for a true 0; mean sigma2 0.98 and 0.91 for a true 1).

  • trait_rates(): shift_rate draws shifts as a Poisson process along the branches, as under the prior of BAMM, so they can fall within branches and the rate of a branch is its mean over time; relative = FALSE gives each new regime a rate of its own, as in BAMM and bifrost, instead of multiplying the rate before the shift; shift_size can be a function that draws the multipliers. data-raw/validation_bamm.R runs BAMM 2.5.0 on 20 trees of 100 tips with about seven such shifts each (10 million generations, lowest effective sample size 62): the mean posterior rate per branch correlated with the true rate (Spearman 0.51, Pearson 0.67 on the log scale), and the marginal probability of a shift was 0.18 on branches with a true shift against 0.02 on the others.

  • trait_rates() simulates a continuous trait whose rate varies among branches and keeps the rates, as the known truth for methods that estimate rates per branch. Three models: shifts at a few branches, inherited by their descendants or not ("shift"); a logarithm of the rate that evolves by Brownian motion ("gbm"); and independent lognormal rates ("iid"). It gives the trait at tips and nodes, the rate of each branch and the rescaled tree.

  • trait_mk(): alpha multiplies the rates of each branch by a gamma factor with mean 1, the model of phytools::fitgammaMk(), or edge_rates gives the factors; rate_classes adds hidden rate classes, as in corHMM, and keeps the hidden history in $hidden. Without them the results are the same as before with the same seed.

  • data-raw/validation_rates.R compares the truth with RRphylo, phytools::multirateBM(), traitMedusa (motmot), fitgammaMk() and corHMM. With one change per branch, rates per branch are weakly identifiable: the Spearman correlation between the true change and the true rate of a branch was 0.29 to 0.40, and RRphylo rates followed the change (0.32 to 0.38) but hardly the rate (0.07 to 0.13). multirateBM recovered the log rates at nodes with r = 0.62 and slope 0.46. traitMedusa found a true eightfold shift in 20 of 30 trees, with a median estimated multiplier of 8.3. fitgammaMk gave a median alpha of 0.33 for a true 0.3 (500 tips), and corHMM preferred two hidden classes in 10 of 12 trees with classes and in none of 12 without.

  • simulate_metacommunity() and mc_dynamics(): immigration = "multinomial" distributes the emigrants of each site among the others by the dispersal kernel and conserves them, as mcomsimr does, on spatially explicit landscapes. The default stays "poisson", as in the code of Thompson et al. (2020). With extirpation 0.02 and dispersal 0.001 on a grid, mean local richness was 1.51 with Poisson, 1.61 with multinomial and 1.61 in mcomsimr.

  • purrr moved from Imports to Suggests: it only gives the progress bar of long loops in interactive sessions. The package now imports only ape and base packages.

comdynamite 0.6.3

  • species_traits(): optima, sigma and r_max take values from elsewhere, such as mvMORPH, by species name or in the order of the species. The traits not given are drawn as before, and with the same seed they are the same as without the external ones. rescale_optima = FALSE keeps external optima on their own scale.
  • Herodotools: as_herodotools() gives its inputs from a simulation or an mc_data object, with the true ancestral areas from a history of trait_mk(); region_pool() limits each species to the sites of its region; arrival_ages() gives the true ages at which lineages arrived in each region. The article “Known biogeographic histories for Herodotools” shows the steps and the results of data-raw/validation_herodotools.R.
  • Trait histories along the tree, to validate reconstructions: trait_bm(nodes = TRUE) and species_traits(nodes = TRUE) give the values at the internal nodes, drawn after everything else so that the other values stay the same with the same seed; traits_ou() keeps them as the attribute nodes. trait_mk() simulates a discrete trait under the Mk model and keeps every change, in the simmap format of phytools. tip_history_metrics() gives the tip-based metrics of Luza et al. (2021), as computed by Herodotools, from a known history, plus the number of changes and the time since the last one in continuous time.
  • simulate_metacommunity() and mc_dynamics(): pool limits each species to the sites where it can occur, such as its range or a biogeographic reconstruction, and initial gives the abundances or presences at the start. Without them, results with the same seed are the same as before.
  • summary_stats(): new statistic trait_k, Blomberg’s K of the trait over the species shared by trait and tree, as picante::Kcalc() gives it. It is NA without a tree or a trait.

comdynamite 0.6.2

  • mc_data() and as_mc_data(): community, tree, traits, environment, coordinates, areas and time series in one object, with names checked once. The analyses and summary_stats() take an mc_data object as first argument and fill what the call leaves out. Simulations keep the tree their traits came from, as tree.
  • run_scenarios(): grids of scenarios with replicates paired by what setup draws, a seed per cell and optional parallel runs.
  • equilibrium_check(): warns when a simulation is still changing at the end of its record.
  • as.data.frame() for mc_sim: long table from history.
  • trait_partition() with site_permutations: each set of predictors now moves alone in its tests, with the response and the other set in place: env for ab, a and its semipartials, space for bc, c and its semipartials; abc still moves both. Up to 0.6.1 the moves took both sets together in every test, which for c compared space with an environment that no longer explained anything: on a grid it rejected 22% of data sets with a strong environment without structure and never with a structured one. In data-raw/validation_fractions_null.R (choice on one generator, check on another), moving env alone rejected a in 3.7% to 7.1% of data sets where the environment had no effect, where free permutations reached 20% with an environment structured outside space, and moving space alone rejected c in 3.0% to 8.0% of null data sets, where free permutations reached 24% with a strong, structured environment. When the environment acts on a trait other than the one analysed, the test of sites of a still rejects, in 45% to 75%, as with free permutations: read p_max, which stayed at 2% to 4%. The power of that test of c was complete for a field in the span of space and 25% to 28% for a field that space holds only in part, since the maps moved around the grid explain such a field about as well: it asks whether the maps in space matter beyond the same maps elsewhere, not whether the remainder has any spatial structure. The result records permutations$moved and the print says which set moves. Free permutations are unchanged.
  • Permutations of pcc_test(), pcps_test(), phylo_beta_test() and trait_partition() run in parallel under a plan of the future package, which is optional.
  • Install from r-universe, as the README now shows.
  • summary_stats(): the same statistics for simulated and observed data, covering diversity, occupancy, abundance distribution, SES MPD and MNTD, distance decay, trait-environment relation and, with more than one step, temporal variation.
  • pcps_test(): principal coordinates of phylogenetic structure of Duarte et al. (2016), the method of the package PCPS, with tests of all the dissimilarity and of each axis, and site_permutations for a restricted null model, which that package does not have. Its statistics match those of PCPS 1.0.9 (data-raw/validation_pcps.R). With autocorrelated fields unrelated to each other, free permutations of sites rejected 29-80% at the 5% level; the torus rejected 4-7% when fields wrap around the grid and 6-25% when they stop at its edges.
  • torus_permutations(): rectangular grids, with side of length two, and new symmetries and n_perm.

comdynamite 0.6.1

  • trait_partition(): the tests of fractions a and c, and of the semipartials, now use the share of the component that the other set leaves unexplained as statistic, which is monotone in the partial F, instead of the fraction itself, which the original code tests. The permutations are the same. The old test lost its power when the other set explained much: in data-raw/validation_fractions.R it rejected a in none of 500 data sets where the environment had no effect and space a strong one (new: 5.6% to 5.8%), and in 15% where the environment had a weak effect beside space (new: 100%). fractions has a new column statistic, and p-values are NA when a fraction cannot be estimated. See the validation article for the limits: a free permutation of sites rejects a too often when env has structure at scales outside space, and site_permutations are nearly degenerate for c.
  • trait_partition(): test of the shared fraction b with shared_null, by Moran spectral randomisation of env from coords (adespatial) or by moves of env alone with site_permutations, as in adespatial::envspace.test(). b is tested only when env is related to space (level), and the result has shared. plot_trait_partition() colours b by its test when there is one.
  • as.data.frame(), summary() and plot() methods for the results of the analyses.
  • rigid_permutations(): restricted null model for the events of node_test() that moves the whole event by a rotation or a reflection and a translation, so it keeps the shape of the sides and the distance between them. It is better than patch_permutations() for sides with room to move, and gives few or no placements for events that span the landscape. Its independent argument covers those at the price of an assumption on the range of autocorrelation, and remains liberal in some layouts. See its help for the rates.
  • rigid_permutations() off a regular lattice now enumerates the moves, on a grid of rotations and reflections with a translation to each site, instead of drawing them at random, so which placements exist no longer changes between runs. In data-raw/validation_offgrid.R it rejected 4.7% and 5.9% of the tests at the 5% level for adjacent areas off a lattice, and 6.8% to 8.0% for two blocks placed at random, where it is liberal.
  • rigid_permutations() and patch_permutations(): the default gap follows the fourth nearest site, the step of a full grid and the spacing of sparse sites, instead of the nearest one. rigid_permutations() thus no longer stops on a grid with holes, and the holes between sites count as inside the landscape while the rim beyond an edge does not. The default of patch_permutations() is unchanged on a full grid where most sites are off the edge, and larger with sparse or irregular sites, where it changes the patches and the results: with 25% to 40% of the sites of a square and areas in opposite corners it rejected 5.6% to 5.9%, against 15% to 17% before (data-raw/validation_gap.R).
  • rigid_permutations() draws the placements at random when an event has more than n_perm of them. Before, with fewer than twice n_perm, it took the first ones in the order of enumeration.
  • node_test(): permutations$areas now gives the number of permutations of each event, which may differ, and print() shows them.
  • plot_phylo_beta(): community matrix with sites ordered by phylo_beta_test() and species by the tree, as Peres-Neto & Kembel (2015) suggest.
  • node_test(): r2_weighted, which stays between 0 and 1, unlike r2, inherited from the original code; n_draws, the valid draws of sites. Errors in parallel workers now stop the function. The default of n_perm is 999, as in the other functions.
  • trait_partition(): site_permutations.
  • pcc_test(), phylo_beta_test(), phylo_vector() and trait_partition() accept empty sites with site_permutations, since these sites are part of the landscape.
  • The significance level is now level in phylo_vector(), plot_node_test(), plot_node_heatmap() and plot_trait_partition(), because alpha also names the competition matrix. alpha still works, with a warning.
  • Names of results, which break code that reads them: p_taxa is now p_species, p_partial_taxa is p_partial_species, and p_partial, the larger of two p-values, is p_partial_max, as in p_max. r2 of pcc_test() is r2_mean and that of phylo_beta_test() is r2_adjusted, which say what they hold. In node_test() and trait_partition(), r2 is unchanged. statistic stays, as the test statistic of each function.
  • phylo_vector(): predictor is now env, as in the other functions, and plot_trait_partition(): test = "taxa" is now "species". The old forms work, with a warning.
  • patch_permutations(): evaluated with autocorrelation up to the scale of the landscape, and advice on gap for sparse sites. The rates given in 0.6.0 averaged over random places of areas. With fixed areas the test is liberal for sides far apart (6% to 10% at the 5% level) and conservative for neighbouring sides, and the help now says so.
  • simulate_metacommunity() matches alpha to traits by name. Before, a matrix with species in another order gave wrong results without warning.
  • growth_rates(), simulate_static() and simulate_metacommunity() accept traits as a matrix or a tibble, and species without names are called sp1, sp2, … simulate_static() matches sets of traits by name. assemble_community() warns when it invents names.
  • Predictors must vary among occupied sites with site_permutations.
  • Help: weights of node_test(), and what the tests of fractions of trait_partition() ask.
  • pcc_test() gives an r2 of 0, not NaN, when no adjusted R2 is positive.
  • node_contrasts() accepts clades with branches of length zero, and plot_node_heatmap() accepts a predictor and an event with the same name.
  • Clearer errors in simulate_metacommunity(), mc_dynamics() with one site, logistic_gradients() and plot_node_heatmap() without tested nodes.

comdynamite 0.6.0

  • patch_permutations(): restricted null model for the events of node_test() in landscapes with edges, which moves the patches of each area and keeps their number and size. It rejected 3.0% to 6.3% of tests at the 5% level in data-raw/validation_edges.R, against 44% to 55% with free permutations.
  • node_test(): area_permutations takes one matrix of permutations per event.
  • New title and description, since the package now covers analyses as well as simulations.
  • ?comdynamite and the README map questions to functions, and the reference and articles on the website are grouped by question.
  • New articles: “Preparing your data” and “Testing the whole tree”, on pcc_test() and phylo_beta_test().

comdynamite 0.5.2

  • biogeography_matrix(): events of node_test() from the area of each site, as pairs of areas stated in advance or as each area against the others.
  • node_test(): site_permutations gives a restricted null model. For events, it moves the areas across the sites.
  • plot_node_test(): biogeographic events are triangles, as in Leibold & Chase (2018).
  • plot_trait_partition(): two overlapping bars along the total variation, as in Figure 1 of Desdevises et al. (2003), so that the shared fraction is seen as shared. New labels.
  • Progress bars with an estimate of the time left in node_test(), pcc_test(), phylo_beta_test(), phylo_vector() and trait_partition(), in interactive sessions.
  • Examples, README and vignettes use trees of treeshapesim, in Suggests. The results of vignette("phylogenetic-structure") and vignette("evaluating-methods") were run again.
  • The help of functions adapted from the MATLAB code of the supplements says so.

Corrections that change results:

  • node_test(): draws are now ranked on F statistics. The statistic of each predictor, taken from the original code, depended on the scale of the response, and neither statistic took into account that draws of species occupy different numbers of sites. p_partial, p_partial_joint, p_taxa, p_max and p_joint differ from those of 0.5.1, and so do the same p-values of events. statistic, p_site and p_partial_site of predictors do not.
  • node_test(): a node with a clade without individuals is no longer tested, as it was a repeat of another node.
  • node_test(): with cores above 1, each call now uses its own random streams.
  • pcc_test() and phylo_beta_test(): species without individuals leave the analysis. In pcc_test() they could turn numerical noise into an axis.
  • trait_partition(): species without individuals leave the analysis, which could stop it.

Checks of data:

  • All analysis functions match sites by name when the data have row names, and stop if the names differ. Before, misordered predictors gave a wrong result without warning.
  • Missing values, predictors without variance and columns that are not numeric now stop with a message that names them. phylo_vector() gave p = 1 in these cases.
  • node_test() checks biogeography before the permutations and explains a tree in nodes.
  • Results keep the numbers of permutations and the null model, and print() shows them with the smallest possible p-value. Nodes that were not tested are reported, and phylo_vector() says when no vector was retained.

comdynamite 0.5.1

  • node_contrasts(): branch_lengths = TRUE gives the coding with branch lengths of the supplement of Leibold et al. (2010).
  • plot_node_test(): with type = "fan", the names of the variables follow the radii and no longer overlap the names of the species.
  • plot_node_heatmap(): semipartial correlations of node_test() as a table of nodes by variables.
  • simulate_logistic() now uses the values of the code of Ives & Helmus (2011): the default of intercept_sd is 0.5, and slopes have a standard deviation of slope_sd among species.
  • logistic_gradients(): in scenario 3, the error is added to y with unit variance and only in y_test, and in scenarios 5 and 6 x is in random order along the transect.
  • New article on analysing clades and traits. The article on validation now compares Table 5 of Peres-Neto et al. (2012).

comdynamite 0.5.0

  • simulate_static(): static metacommunities from the Gaussian response of Dray & Legendre (2008), also used by Peres-Neto et al. (2012), as a baseline without population dynamics. Data can be Poisson counts, binomial presences or the expected values. With several gradients, for example environment and space, the expected abundance is the product of the responses.
  • simulate_logistic() and logistic_gradients(): presences and absences from logistic responses to two gradients, with the seven scenarios of Appendix C of Peres-Neto et al. (2012).
  • phylo_vector() and trait_partition(): phylogenetic gradient analysis of Peres-Neto et al. (2012), tested against the original code in Octave. The test between a trait and the environment stays in ade4::fourthcorner().
  • Functions that take a community and a phylogeny, traits or contrasts now match species by name and, as picante::match.phylo.comm(), drop with a warning the species found in only one of them. Repeated names are an error.
  • trait_partition(): semipartial correlations of each predictor, with their tests, following Appendix A of Peres-Neto et al. (2012).
  • plot_node_test(): results of node_test() on the tree, as in Figure 3 of Leibold et al. (2010), as a phylogram or a fan. plot_trait_partition(): fractions of trait_partition().
  • daphniids: data of Leibold et al. (2010), rebuilt from the public survey.
  • node_contrasts() now keeps nodes that join two tips, as the article does. cherries = FALSE gives the original code.
  • node_test(): semipartial replaces partial_r2, following the article, and there are p_adjusted (false discovery rate), biogeographic events, the joint permutation of the article (p_joint), 9999 permutations by default and cores.
  • pcc_test() and phylo_eigenvectors(): phylogenetic community composition of Peres-Neto & Kembel (2015), with site and species permutations.
  • phylo_beta_test() and phylo_beta(): phylogenetic beta-diversity framework of the same article, a distance-based redundancy analysis of the mean phylogenetic distance between communities.
  • node_test() and node_contrasts(): regression of clades on the environment, node by node, from Leibold et al. (2010), with site and species permutations.
  • simulate_metacommunity() and mc_dynamics(): stochastic extirpation of populations (extirpation), used by Thompson et al. (2020) in their competition-colonisation scenario.
  • New article on the validation of the model, with the differences between the article of Thompson et al. (2020) and the code archived with it.
  • New article with animations of metacommunity dynamics.

comdynamite 0.1.0

  • First version: the model of Thompson et al. (2020) with phylogenetic traits and competition, spatially implicit and grid landscapes, torus permutations and time-varying environments. Code from the pcps-sim project.

  • Rule-based assembly (assemble_community()): limiting similarity (GAUSE algorithm of Colwell & Winkler 1984), habitat filtering and neutral assembly, as in Kraft et al. (2007).

  • traits_ou(): traits under an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with one or several optima (multi-peak OU; Brownian motion when alpha = 0), with paint_regimes() to assign regimes to clades.

  • New vignettes: vignette("phylogenetic-structure"), on how dispersal, niche conservatism and competition shape phylogenetic community structure, and vignette("evaluating-methods"), on type I error and power with simulations.

  • vignette("evaluating-methods") shows tree shape as a factor of the design, with trees from treeshapesim (in Suggests).
